1) the genetic architecture of tolerance to a lignocellulose inhibitor is complex, 2) the tolerance phenotype is the product of a combination of driver mutations and hitchhikers, 3) there is evidence for compensatory evolution, and 4) historical contingency plays an important role in shaping the outcome of genome shuffling.

we performed whole population whole-genome resequencing on a genome shuffling experiment, identified driver and hitchhiker mutations and explored the impact of historical genetic drift on the outcomes of the experiment.

the genetic basis of phenotypic evolution and the impact of evolutionary engineering methodologies on the genetic architecture of traits.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic architecture of inhibitor tolerance is highly complex and that the evolutionary dynamics of the GS experiment were influenced by historical contingency.

genome shuffling is an effective tool for the evolution of complex phenotypes, but that it is important to be aware of the limitations imposed by the experimental design and the underlying biology of the system.
our work demonstrates that whole population whole genome sequencing and phenotypic assays can provide a powerful tool for the dissection of complex evolutionary outcomes in industrial microorganisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the evolutionary engineering of complex phenotypes in industrial strains of S. cerevisiae is a highly complex process, and that the outcomes of genome shuffling experiments are highly sensitive to the starting strain, the selection regime and the mutagenesis protocol used.
the genetic architecture of our evolved strain is complex, and the evolutionary dynamics of our experiment are driven by the interplay of selection and genetic drift.
the genetic basis for inhibitor tolerance in GS strains of S. cerevisiae is complex, with multiple mutations contributing to the phenotype and epistasis playing a role.
The main takeaway from our work is that

evolutionary experiments can be used to identify the molecular determinants underlying complex phenotypes and the genetic architecture of complex traits, even in the absence of prior knowledge of the underlying molecular mechanisms.
the evolutionary engineering process is not deterministic and that the outcomes of a genome shuffling experiment are strongly influenced by the genetic background of the starting population.
the genetic architecture of evolved phenotypes can be inferred using a combination of genomic and experimental data.
